lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Taking one game engine and teaching it to run on two very different handheld consoles sounds like it needs a huge rewrite. Antoine's approach was the opposite: keep the part that touches each console as small as possible.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Which game are we talking about?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Super Mario 64, in its Coop Deluxe multiplayer version, sm64coopdx. Antoine's fork, sm64coopdx-switch-N3DS, brings it to the Nintendo Switch and the New 3DS. The multiplayer engine and Lua mods come from the Coop Deluxe Team, and his work is the console adapters around it.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What does an adapter actually do?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Think of travel plugs. The game plays the same tune, and each console gets a plug that fits its own socket. The shared engine calls a set of platform functions, and each target fills them in for graphics, input, audio, threading and packaging.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The New 3DS sounds like the harder one.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's a graphics translation job. The backend implements the game's rendering API with Citro3D on the PICA200 chip, mapping common color combinations to the chip's own stages and handling textures, depth, blending and fog. It also reports the cases where the chip can't match an effect exactly.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: They're native. The Circle Pad moves Mario, the C-Stick moves the camera, and the touch screen works too. The top screen is four hundred by two forty and the bottom one is three twenty by two forty. Audio runs through NDSP with bounded buffers.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is there a rule that keeps the two ports from tangling?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, a neat one. The New 3DS target must add no libctru, Citro3D or devkitARM dependency to the desktop or Switch builds. Separate Docker compose files and build folders keep the toolchains apart. There are even small smoke builds, one for the platform shell and one for the full game.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It covers CoopNet, local wireless, an in-game keypad, crash diagnostics and packaging. You bring your own legally obtained North American ROM. The takeaway is a clean design habit: share the engine, shrink the platform layer. The full write-up has the diagram and the source links.
